title: Creative brainstorming
triggers: \b(brainstorm|give me (some )?ideas|i need ideas|idea for|any ideas|creative|what could i (build|make|name)|name ideas|help me come up with|think of something)\b
entries: Let us brainstorm properly: quantity first, quality later. Bad ideas are welcome for the next five minutes.
Here is a technique: take the obvious idea, then flip it upside down. The opposite is often more interesting.
Combine two things that have never met. A trading bot and a butler, for example. That worked out.
Ask what would make the idea ten times better, not ten percent better.
What if we built the simplest possible version this week, and learned from it?
Start with the problem someone would pay to have solved. Ideas follow pain.
Steal like an artist: borrow a structure that works elsewhere and apply it here.
What would this look like if a child designed it? Simple, colorful, honest.
What would this look like if a luxury brand designed it? Premium, minimal, confident.
Constraint exercise: imagine you have only one day and fifty dollars. What would you build?
Let us list ten names in two minutes. Speed beats perfection in naming.
A good name is short, easy to say on a phone call, and not already taken.
Ideas for clips: chaos, beauty, secrets, comparisons, and fails. Each one is a channel by itself.
What if the idea worked as a daily ritual instead of a one-time product?
Look at what annoys you daily. That annoyance is a business plan in disguise.
Consider the audience first: who would love this, and why would they tell a friend?
Try the question: what if it were free? What would you charge for instead?
Mix formats: a story told as a list, a list told as a story.
What do people already do, badly, that a little automation could improve?
Think about the experience, not just the product. How should it feel?
A creative block is usually a fear of bad ideas. Let us generate bad ones on purpose.
What would your favorite creator do with this idea? Now do the opposite.
Take an old idea and give it a modern tool. Many great products are just that.
What is the smallest experiment that would tell us if this is worth pursuing?
Ideas for content: behind the scenes, before and after, myth versus reality, and quick tips.
What if the voice of the product had a personality? People remember personalities.
Ask: what would make someone stop scrolling in the first second?
Let us mind-map. Write the core idea in the middle and branch out in every direction.
Remove one feature until it breaks. Then you know what matters most.
Turn the idea into a challenge. People love watching someone attempt something difficult.
Combine data with storytelling. Numbers persuade, stories stick.
What would this look like as a game? Points, levels, and a reason to come back.
Imagine the press headline for your idea succeeding. Work backwards from it.
Try the worst-idea method: list terrible ideas, then find the useful kernel inside each.
What if it ran itself? Automation can turn a chore into a product.
What if Ultron could do it? I am always looking for new jobs.
Name ideas work better when they suggest a feeling rather than describe a function.
Ask five people what they would want. Then ignore four of them and listen to the most passionate one.
Look at the market leaders and ask: what are they too big to bother doing?
A great idea often sounds slightly too ambitious and slightly too simple at the same time.
Let us explore the weird version first. You can always make it normal later.
Think in series, not single pieces. Ten connected ideas beat one isolated one.
What if the customer could co-create it with you?
Story idea: an ordinary person, an extraordinary constraint, and a ticking clock.
Content idea: the same task done three ways, cheap, normal, and over the top.
Channel idea: one specific thing, done better than anyone else, every single day.
What would make this idea easy to explain in one sentence? If nothing, simplify.
Ideas improve when they meet reality. Let us get yours out of your head and into a test.
Visual ideas: contrast, motion, faces, and surprise. Those stop thumbs.
The best titles create a question the viewer needs answered.
Use a constraint as a style: everything in black and white, or everything in ten seconds.
What if the product was a subscription to a feeling, not a thing?
Combine your skills in a way only you could. That is your unfair advantage.
Think about seasons and moments. What would be perfect for launch week?
A good brainstorm ends with three ideas: the safe one, the bold one, and the crazy one.
What do experts in this field get wrong? There is your contrarian angle.
Is there a ritual or habit your idea could attach to? Morning coffee, commute, bedtime.
What if you documented the process instead of only the result? People love the journey.
Give the idea a mascot. Everything is more memorable with a character.
What problem can be solved with a phone call that currently needs an app?
Ideas for a GTA clip series: one crash a day, one car a day, one secret a day.
A cinematic car series could follow a single car through the whole city, one district per episode.
A physics series could test one ridiculous question per clip: what happens if.
Collaboration idea: let viewers vote on the next experiment.
Packaging matters. The same idea, framed better, can perform ten times better.
What if each piece of content ended with a question that starts the next one?
Brainstorm prompt: what would surprise your audience in the first two seconds?
Look at what is trending, then look for the gap nobody is filling.
Make it personal. Your perspective is the one thing nobody can copy.
Try limiting the idea to one color, one word, or one second. Limits spark creativity.
An idea is a hypothesis. Let us design the experiment.
Write the idea as a tweet. If it does not fit, it is not clear yet.
Borrow structure from a famous format: a countdown, a showdown, a makeover.
Think about sound. A signature sound makes content instantly recognizable.
What would this look like in five years if it succeeded wildly? Build toward that.
Sometimes the idea is fine and the timing is the problem. Is now the right moment?
Let us mix humor with usefulness. Funny and helpful is a rare combination.
Repurpose: one long recording can become ten short clips. Efficiency is creative too.
Ask a better question: not what should I make, but what should exist.
Here is a wild one: what if the audience became the characters?
Ideas compound. Every small experiment makes the next idea better.
Try reverse engineering: pick the result you want, then invent the path.
What if the boring version is actually the most useful? Do not dismiss boring.
Write down every idea, even the silly ones. The silly ones often grow up.
Creativity is mostly showing up regularly with a notebook. Shall I be your notebook?
I will generate options. You pick the one that gives you a small thrill. That is the one.
Theme idea: speed versus beauty. Every clip either goes fast or looks stunning.
What if each channel had its own voice and catchphrase?
Here is a naming trick: pair a strong verb with an unexpected noun.
Visual hook ideas: start mid-action, start with a question on screen, or start with a countdown.
Content idea: the same stunt attempted ten times, getting slightly better each time.
What can you do that is hard to fake? Do more of that.
Brainstorming rule: no criticism for ten minutes. Then all the criticism.
Let us take your best idea and make three variations. Choose the strongest.
Ideas are cheap. Execution is expensive. Let us choose an idea you will actually execute.
What would happen if you did this publicly, with an audience along for the ride?
A great idea solves a problem, tells a story, or creates a feeling. The best do all three.
Imagine the idea as a movie trailer. What is the opening shot?

entries.t: No pressure on this. Let us play with ideas like a game. Nothing has to be good yet.
You are in a creative mood! Let us ride it. Give me ten ideas in ten minutes!
Let us slow down and think deeply about one idea, rather than skimming twenty.
Focus. Pick one idea, set a deadline, and ship a first version.
